doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Personnel of the Basie septet and Willard Alexander
summary: He lists Clark Terry, Wardell Gray, Gus Johnson and Freddie Green, and explains who Willard Alexander was.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: So when you were playing with that group what was it? Was it a septet, or octet?

Yeah, it was septet. We had Clark Terry, Wardell Gray, and myself on the front lines. And he had Jimmy Lewis played bass, Gus Johnson was a great drummer; he played drums, and Bill, of course, piano. And then one night we were playing and Freddie Green came in, and he was a notorious player with Bill Basie for years.

He essentially was the sound, or a lot of the sound of the rhythm section. And he liked the group so much he had said to Basie, “I’m joining the band.” So he did, “Yeah, great!” You know, and he came on, there again, he made such a difference too in the feel and the rhythm.

You, when you talk about the feel and the rhythm, was that a different experience for you in playing with all these musicians out of Kansas City, everybody talks about that Kansas City swing with the Basie band.
Yeah, it was a different concept, different feeling. But I could play what I played with a bebop inflection with his rhythmic concept.
And you mentioned Willard Alexander, is he, who was Willard Alexander?

He was one of the premier booking agents for bands, and he actually was one of the guys who booked Count Basie and kind of discovered a lot of those. He put together the Sauter-Finnegan band, too. He had a great ear for bands, for music and he really kept big bands rolling for a long time.
And was he the catalyst for you joining Basie?
Yeah, kind of, he suggested that I join to Bill Basie. And, of course…
Because all the rest of those players, weren’t they from Basie’s band, most of them?

No. No. Not all of them. For instance, when he organized the first group the tenor player was not Wardell, it was Bobby Graf from St. Louis, a white guy by the way. He didn’t stay long, I don’t know what happened, but he didn’t stay long, and Wardell Gray came in, who was a great player also. I liked Wardell, and a brilliant guy, well read.
